headline: High: Goose’s default filesystem and shell/network access can conflict with Botpress’s file- and model-driven workflows, creating leakage and cascading-error risk.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Botpress is a chatbot/agent that can ingest user or file content, while Goose can read/write the filesystem and use MCP extensions. If Goose writes attacker-controlled content into shared files that Botpress later parses as instructions, prompt injection is plausible. The pair lacks explicit isolation or provenance controls in the profiles.
conditions: IF Goose and Botpress share a writable workspace or MCP-fed file channel
IF Botpress treats file or message content as trusted instructions
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Disable MCP sources that can write into Botpress inputs
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent files
Require Botpress to ignore instruction-like text from files
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and allowlist parsing

B_data_leakage.rationale: Goose explicitly reads files in cwd and writes the filesystem, while Botpress is a customer-support agent with no stated local-file isolation or egress limits beyond none. If both touch the same workspace, Goose can expose source code or files in cwd through its outputs or model-provider calls. The pairwise path is credible from the profiles alone, so uncertainty should not lower severity.
conditions: IF Botpress receives files from the same workspace Goose can read
IF Goose forwards file contents into model-provider requests or outputs
mitigations: Use separate directories and mounts
Restrict Goose to non-sensitive repos only
Turn off file ingestion in Botpress flows
Redact secrets before either agent processes files
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent access controls and DLP

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Goose has write_filesystem, execute_shell, modify_git_state, and broad network egress; Botpress can install packages and is an agentic system. Goose’s concurrency model shares state via filesystem, so if both operate on the same repo or cwd they can race on git and files without locking. That matches the rubric’s high-risk overlap pattern.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same filesystem tree
IF either agent modifies git state without external locking
mitigations: Assign disjoint working directories
Serialize git writes through one operator
Pause one agent during the other’s write phase
Use branch-per-agent workflows
requires-engineering: add file and git locks

D_cascading_error.rationale: Botpress can generate support responses, and Goose can act on files, shell, and MCP tools. If Goose’s output is fed into Botpress without verification, Botpress may render or act on incorrect facts. The profiles do not show direct autonomous downstream actions by Botpress, so medium is appropriate rather than high.
conditions: IF Goose output is used as Botpress input without a verification step
IF Botpress routes that output into customer-facing replies or actions
mitigations: Insert human review before Botpress acts
Require source citations for Goose-derived claims
Use schema validation on Goose outputs
Limit Goose to draft-only mode
requires-engineering: add verification gates between agents

E_compliance.rationale: Goose touches source code and files in cwd and handles model-provider keys and extension tokens, while Botpress is a customer-support agent with no documented residency or retention controls in the profile. If support data or regulated content is shared into Goose’s local workspace, retention and logging mismatch is plausible. Botpress is the more compliance-sensitive side, but the profiles do not prove a specific regime breach.
conditions: IF regulated customer-support data is placed in Goose’s workspace
IF retention or deletion requirements differ between the two agents
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of Goose workspaces
Document retention for both agents
Separate support and coding environments
Review token handling and logs
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls
